items.title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
items.summary: The chancellor targets the cost of living amid global economic turmoil but opposition parties say he has not been bold enough.
items.body: Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget. The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms". He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

items.title: Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m households
items.summary: Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis Budget 2026: key points at a glance Briefing: key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa Crerar Editorial: Budget’s bold ambitions and…
items.body: John Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund a £100 winter handout for 20 million families as official forecasts made clear there is no end in sight for the cost of living crisis. In his first budget, the chancellor blamed “global economic storms” for the grim outlook, as the war in Iran drives up oil and gas prices. But he also faced criticism for failing to squeeze more money from profitable banks, punishing savers and not giving enough help to the poorest. In a low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, Healey was at pains to stress he was sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, and there were few surprises in his hour-long address to MPs.

items.title: EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers
items.summary: In shielding Europe's carmakers from Chinese rivals, the EU risks hurting close partners from Turkey and Morocco to Japan and South Korea. Billions in trade and hundreds of thousands of European jobs are at stake.
items.body: It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) , proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe. Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey , Morocco , Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains. After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status. Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

items.title: From hairy crabs to soybeans, China looks to vast salt-affected wastelands for agriculture
items.summary: As China enters autumn, a dark, furry-clawed crustacean – no larger than a human palm – becomes one of the most sought-after delicacies in the country. Chinese hairy crabs, a national obsession traditionally raised in the freshwater lakes of the Yangtze River Delta, are now…
items.body: As China enters autumn, a dark, furry-clawed crustacean – no larger than a human palm – becomes one of the most sought-after delicacies in the country. Chinese hairy crabs, a national obsession traditionally raised in the freshwater lakes of the Yangtze River Delta, are now being farmed on a stretch of salt-affected alkaline wasteland in the northwest province of Shaanxi. The area along Yellow River floodplains is unsuitable for conventional crops, but farmers have transformed over 600 hectares (1,482 acres) for hairy crab cultivation, generating an estimated total output value of 90 million yuan (US$13.5 million), the People’s Daily website reported on Tuesday.

items.title: Alphabet sinks 10% as it holds 2026 capex unchanged, expects significant increase in 2027
items.summary: Alphabet missed Q3 expectations on earnings and revenue, its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years.
items.body: Alphabet shares slumped more than 10% after the search giant reported a drop in free cash flow during the third quarter, in a worrying sign for the artificial intelligence trade. Revenue grew 25% from a year ago, but the company posted its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years. Net income fell to $26.17 billion, or $2.12 per share, down from $34.98 billion, or $2.87 per share, a year ago. The Google parent reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, which fell much further than the $2.70 billion expected by analysts. As questions mount over heightened spending on the AI buildout, Alphabet's capital expenditures totaled $51.36 billion in Q3, falling short of the $55.09 billion expected by analysts. Investors are looking for a substantial return on investment to warrant the big spending plans from the hyperscalers.

items.title: Bessent says 'not necessarily' a mistake if the Fed hikes again
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joined CNBC for an interview on Oct. 28, 2026.
items.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that further Federal Reserve rate hikes wouldn't necessarily be a mistake. After CNBC's Brian Sullivan asked if rate increases in the future would constitute a monetary policy error, Bessent responded: "That's not necessarily so." Bessent's comments came hours after the Fed announced it would keep interest rates unchanged at its October gathering, as the market widely expected. Bessent is a key confidant of President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. Trump pressured Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's predeccesor, Jerome Powell, over the issue during Powell's final months at the helm of the central bank. But Bessent said Wednesday that both he and Trump believe Warsh is doing well and can strike a balance between ensuring full employment and stable prices. "I think Chair Warsh is off to a great start," Bessent said.

He says the administration will have a new approach, to steer us through global economic storms and give people fresh hope for Britain’s future. The UK did not want this war, and it has driven up costs for British families through higher energy costs and higher interest rates.

items.summary: China’s Yangtze River Delta grew faster than the national economy in the first three quarters of the year, accounting for about a quarter of national output – a performance analysts said would help lay the foundation for Beijing to meet its annual national growth target. But…
items.body: China’s Yangtze River Delta grew faster than the national economy in the first three quarters of the year, accounting for about a quarter of national output – a performance analysts said would help lay the foundation for Beijing to meet its annual national growth target. But they also cautioned that exports and hi-tech manufacturing alone could not sustain longer-term growth without a recovery in sluggish domestic demand. The combined gross domestic product of Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui, which together make up the Yangtze River Delta region in eastern China, reached about 26.75 trillion yuan (US$4 trillion) in the first three quarters, according to regional government data. Zhejiang, home to the export hub of Yiwu and major companies including e-commerce giant Alibaba Group Holding and carmaker Geely, recorded the fastest growth at 5.6 per cent year on year.

items.title: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine
items.summary: Healey presented his first budget as Chancellor, and reiterated the UK's support of Ukraine on Wednesday.
items.body: The U.K. has set out a target date for defense spending to rise to 3% of GDP, as the finance minister announced billions in aid for Ukraine in a "clear message to Moscow". John Healey on Wednesday set a target date of 2030 for the 3% figure, while reaffirming its NATO commitment to reach 3.5% by 2035 . Healey, who resigned as defense minister under the previous government over insufficient spending, presented his first annual budget as finance minister and highlighted a "new era of threat". "Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said as he announced an additional £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in economic and military support, based on loans, export finance guarantees, as well as £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter.

items.title: The UK cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defense in high-stakes budget
items.summary: The U.K. budget cuts household energy costs, raises taxes on banks and directs billions toward defense, Ukraine and artificial intelligence
items.body: The U.K.'s finance minister John Healey delivered his first fiscal budget on Wednesday, announcing funding for defense, AI initiatives and measures designed to ease cost-of-living pressures. The Autumn Budget included dozens of measures aimed largely at easing rising costs for Britain's population, but Healey was careful not to risk the ire of markets, which responded broadly positively to his plans. Inflation has risen sharply this year, with surging fuel costs driving the annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September. Markets expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month, while government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year. The U.K. government, led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, had promised to alleviate economic pressures ahead of the budget.

items.title: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out
items.summary: The chancellor announced a series of measures which will impact under-25 year-olds from housing to minimum wage.
items.body: Chancellor John Healey has announced his Budget, which includes changes to minimum wage and help for people trying to get onto the housing ladder. If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April. However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people. Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

items.title: ‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget
items.summary: OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’ Budget 2026: key points at a glance Budget 2026 live – latest updates British households face a…
items.body: British households face a “grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said. As John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued its report showing a sharp downgrade for growth in 2027, household disposable incomes and the public finances, despite the measures taken by the chancellor . Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help with soaring energy costs, the watchdog said household disposable incomes after taking account of inflation would fall by 0.6% next year. The downgrade - compared with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes that the OBR was forecasting in March – was driven mainly by higher energy costs.

items.title: China’s private sector wages waver as gap widens with non-private firms
items.summary: The wide gulf in average annual wages between China’s private and non-private sectors continued to expand in 2025, while regional disparities also remained stark, with Tibet continuing to outshine some coastal provinces in income levels. The findings, based on the latest data…
items.body: The wide gulf in average annual wages between China’s private and non-private sectors continued to expand in 2025, while regional disparities also remained stark, with Tibet continuing to outshine some coastal provinces in income levels. The findings, based on the latest data released by the National Bureau of Statistics this week, underscore the yawning sectoral and regional divides in the world’s second-largest economy. Workers in China’s non-private sector – including government and state-owned enterprise employees as well as workers at entities run by foreign, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwanese investors – earned an average of 129,441 yuan (US$19,415) in 2025, up 4.3 per cent year on year. That was 80 per cent higher than the average wage of 71,590 yuan in the private sector, where income grew 3 per cent year on year. The gap widened to 57,851 yuan in 2025 from 48,792 yuan in 2022.

items.title: How Lao Gan Ma, China’s iconic chilli brand, got caught in an AI storm
items.summary: For three decades, Lao Gan Ma’s glass jars, bearing the stern portrait of founder Tao Huabi, have been a fixture on Chinese dinner tables and a symbol of traditional food manufacturing. This week, however, the iconic chilli sauce has become an unlikely focus of public anxiety…
items.body: For three decades, Lao Gan Ma’s glass jars, bearing the stern portrait of founder Tao Huabi, have been a fixture on Chinese dinner tables and a symbol of traditional food manufacturing. This week, however, the iconic chilli sauce has become an unlikely focus of public anxiety over artificial intelligence. Online rumours that the Guizhou-based company had replaced hundreds of factory workers with AI went viral, prompting boycott threats and highlighting growing public unease over the impact of automation on jobs in the world’s second-largest economy. Speculation mounted on the social media platform Weibo on Monday after claims spread that Lao Gan Ma had reduced its chilli-sorting workforce from more than 600 people to just 48 after installing an AI-powered inspection system.

items.title: At least 68 people dead in high-speed Spain train crash
items.summary: It is the second deadly high-speed train collision in Spain this year.
items.body: At least 68 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, authorities have said. The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line. Transport Minister Óscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the control system at the nearby town of Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart and travelled 25km before hitting a stopped train at high speed, he added, saying it was "inexplicable" how this had happened. Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported .

items.title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
items.summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
items.body: John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path. It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help. While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain. The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes. Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament.

items.summary: Chancellor fleshes out details of scheme unveiled last month to help 70,000 households on to the property ladder Budget 2026: key points at a glance Income tax: How much more will you pay? Nils Pratley: Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try A new £4.7bn government…
items.body: A new £4.7bn government scheme will help 70,000 households on to the property ladder and save first-time buyers “hundreds of pounds a month”, the chancellor, John Healey, said on Wednesday. Last month, Andy Burnham announced Your First Home , which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers in England who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”, and Healey revealed in his first budget how the scheme would work, including who would be eligible. You could argue Your First Home (YFH) is effectively an updated version of the Conservatives’ flagship help to buy scheme, which ended in 2023. YFH applies to England only and is just for prospective first-time buyers hoping to buy a new-build flat or house. Those taking part, who buy a home from a participating developer, will be offered a government-backed “equity loan” worth 20% of the purchase price.

A typical yearly energy bill is forecast to jump by £276 in January , according to consultants Cornwall Insight. Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said. items.title: Income tax: Healey’s budget leaves thresholds frozen again. How much more will you pay?
items.summary: Tax policy means freezes reduce take-home pay as earnings rise in line with inflation Income tax thresholds are set to remain frozen after John Healey’s first budget as chancellor. One of the biggest tax rises in recent years has happened without a change in the rates at which…
items.body: Income tax thresholds are set to remain frozen after John Healey’s first budget as chancellor. One of the biggest tax rises in recent years has happened without a change in the rates at which people are taxed on their incomes. Instead it has come from successive government decisions to keep the thresholds associated with the tax at the same level each year, regardless of inflation. Freezing tax thresholds results in “fiscal drag” – a phenomenon where people are dragged into higher tax bands when they get pay rises. Until 2021, the UK income tax thresholds were typically increased each year in line with inflation. When the then chancellor, Rishi Sunak, delivered his budget that year he announced that thresholds would be frozen from April 2022 until 2026 .

items.title: Elon Musk is a 'real genius', Putin says after satellite talks with SpaceX boss
items.summary: The Russian President praised Musk and said they are in "close" contact.
items.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has promoted the country's own satellite internet project. Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology. The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites. "He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk." Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment. Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

items.title: Business secretary writes to Poundland owner as administration fears build
items.summary: Jonathan Reynolds’ team has written to Gordon Brothers, which bought retailer for £1 last summer, to ‘establish the facts’ The business secretary’s team has written to the owner of Poundland amid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening…
items.body: The business secretary’s team has written to the owner of Poundland amid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening to overshadow John Healey’s budget. Sources said that Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm that bought the 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, looks set to appoint administrators to the struggling retailer. Jonathan Reynolds has written to Gordon Brothers to establish the latest situation at the company, which employs 12,000 staff. The company rejected the only bid to take on the group – which includes the 50-store Dealz chain in Ireland – as a solvent company in its entirety, from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, earlier this week. It is understood Gordon Brothers is poised to file a notice of intention to appoint the advisory firm AlixPartners as administrator, potentially as early as Wednesday.

items.title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
items.summary: The point at which you start to pay tax, and the point where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax have been frozen for three more years.
items.body: Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation. John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end. The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets. But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.

items.title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
items.summary: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3% The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the…
items.body: The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years. Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement. Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%. Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.

items.title: Ford reports mixed third-quarter results, says 2027 earnings will be in line with this year
items.summary: Ford Motor reported earnings that beat Wall Street’s estimates but slightly missed on revenue.
items.body: DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter. The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year. "This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday. Ford reported third-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $4.7 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than what analysts were anticipating, according to StreetAccount.

items.title: Give UK workers right to know colleagues’ pay to prevent disparities, says watchdog
items.summary: EHRC says transparency needed to prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women Workers should have a legal right to know their colleagues’ pay to help prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women, the UK’s human rights watchdog has said. The Equality and Human…
items.body: Workers should have a legal right to know their colleagues’ pay to help prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women, the UK’s human rights watchdog has said. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) made the recommendation in response to government proposals to overhaul equal pay laws, saying workers deserved a right to transparency if they suspected other staff were being paid more for similar work. The watchdog also said bosses should be banned from asking about applicants’ existing salaries when recruiting staff. Companies are currently allowed to request that information, but potential recruits do not have to respond. Ministers are considering forcing bosses to respond to staff questionnaires about their colleagues’ pay, reintroducing a right that was abolished in 2014 as part of a drive to cut bureaucracy for businesses.

items.title: Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
items.summary: The reduction in public spending will go towards paying for the Defence Investment Plan.
items.body: Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan. The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag. The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding: "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now." Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".

items.title: ‘Elonville’: US residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noise
items.summary: Several Mississippi homes have been purchased near datacenters and one resident said realtor outlined target to buy more than 400 People in a Mississippi neighborhood, many of whom dislike a nearby power plant central to Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence ambitions, have…
items.body: People in a Mississippi neighborhood, many of whom dislike a nearby power plant central to Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence ambitions, have received a stark offer – to sell their houses to his company and make way. Real estate agents have been going door to door in Southaven, Mississippi , on behalf of xAI, touting a deal to purchase houses as long as the owners agree to not join a lawsuit against the company over the power plant’s noise. (Musk’s AI company officially became SpaceXAI in July and has lately been rebranded as SpaceXSI but to neighbors of the datacenter in Mississippi, it remains xAI.) This plan could potentially swallow up almost the entire neighborhood of Colonial Hills, on the western flank of Southaven.

items.title: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket
items.summary: Cruise operator Villa Vie Residences said it would disembark passengers and crew, and restructure its business due to soaring fuel costs.
items.body: A luxury cruise around the world has abruptly stopped, stranding passengers in Cambodia, as its operator blamed skyrocketing fuel costs. The Villa Vie Odyssey , a luxury vessel with rooms costing up to $11,000 a month, will disembark passengers and crew and find temporary accommodation, per a Tuesday online release. The vessel can carry up to 650 passengers, according to its U.S.-based operator Villa Vie Residences , and has been on a continuous voyage around the world for two years since it departed Belfast, Northern Ireland. Its amenities include a fitness center and spa, a business center, three restaurants, five bars and lounges and complimentary alcoholic beverages. The cruise drew international attention as it was marketed as a residential cruise offering a permanent home at sea while visiting hundreds of destinations.

items.title: GSK shares dive as weaker vaccine sales unnerve investors
items.summary: British pharma company one of biggest fallers on FTSE 100 despite better than expected financial results Business live – latest updates Shares in GSK slid on Wednesday despite the UK drugmaker reporting better than expected financial results, as investors were unnerved by weaker…
items.body: Shares in GSK slid on Wednesday despite the UK drugmaker reporting better than expected financial results, as investors were unnerved by weaker sales of its respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and shingles vaccines and recently launched medications. Britain’s second-biggest pharmaceutical company reported a 19% decline in pre-tax profit to £1.9bn in the July to September quarter and £318m of restructuring charges, with more to come. Core operating profit and core earnings per share rose 5% and 1% respectively, however, beating analysts’ expectations. Shares dived as much as 7% at one point on Wednesday, and despite later paring back such losses to a 3.8% drop, it was the second-biggest faller on the FTSE 100 index of blue-chip businesses.

items.title: Chipotle shares rise 7% after CEO says same-store sales growth will continue
items.summary: For the first time this year, low-income consumers during the quarter outperformed the high-income cohort at its restaurants, CEO Scott Boatwright said.
items.body: Chipotle Mexican Grill on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results and said its restaurant-level operating margin shrank. But the burrito chain saw traffic and same-store sales grow during the quarter as low-income consumers spent more, bucking industry trends, and CEO Scott Boatwright projected a strong finish to the year. "Broader consumer and industry headwinds may continue, but initiatives across our recipe for growth strategy are building and giving us more tools to win in any environment," Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call. "We are still in the early stages of this work, and it's gaining traction." Like the broader restaurant industry, Chipotle saw trends soften in early October, although executives said its traffic has returned to growth since then. Boatwright said the company has "high confidence" in its performance for the rest of the fourth quarter.

items.summary: Employees should legally be able to find out what their co-workers are earning, the UK's equality watchdog says
items.body: Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said. Bosses should be required to respond to questionaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has proposed , external . In addition, employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from carrying on, it said. Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them . At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about colleagues.

items.title: Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs
items.summary: The luxury MV Odyssey ship slated for a years-long voyage around the world suspends operations amid high fuel prices A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia…
items.body: A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia because of high fuel prices. The ship, known as the MV Odyssey, had been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials told the Associated Press . The ship has a 650-passenger capacity. The Florida-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey, the company that operates the cruise line, said it was working with passengers on organizing “temporary living arrangements”. The cruise ship had begun its journey in Belfast in October 2024 for what was described as a “continuous voyage around the world”. “Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” a statement on the company’s website said.

items.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
items.summary: Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40% Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But…
items.body: Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety. Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers. Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track.

items.title: Apple brings touch to the Mac, reversing years-old stance on touchscreen laptop
items.summary: Apple announces a new touchscreen laptop, the company's third major launch under new CEO John Ternus.
items.body: Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display. Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops. It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid. The new laptop will go on sale Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models.

items.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
items.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
items.body: Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said. Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%. The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole. The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say. China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .

items.title: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham
items.summary: Prime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of options Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with…
items.body: Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum. In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this. Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote.

items.title: Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat
items.summary: Microsoft reported better-than-expected results driven by 48% growth in Azure revenue.
items.body: Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business. The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.

items.title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
items.summary: Plans to switch to digital landlines by January could leave remote areas of the UK vulnerable, MPs say.
items.body: Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned. Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year. The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service. But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency. Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

items.title: US lawmakers demand action on overcharging at 7-Eleven, Dollar General and other chains
items.summary: Democrats urge FTC to tackle ‘systemic failure’ of biggest convenience and dollar stores over pricing practices after Guardian investigations Thirty-four members of Congress are calling on the Federal Trade Commission to investigate reports of widespread overcharging by some of…
items.body: Thirty-four members of Congress are calling on the Federal Trade Commission to investigate reports of widespread overcharging by some of America’s most-recognized brand-name retailers. The 28 October letter to the FTC comes in direct response to Guardian investigations of four of the nation’s largest dollar-store and convenience-store chains. Both investigations revealed pervasive mismatches between shelf labels and register prices. The first , published in December, found that Dollar General had failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period on items such as peanut butter, spaghetti sauce and Flintstone vitamins. Its smaller rival, Family Dollar, failed 2,100 price inspections in 20 states over the same period. The second , published last month, found a similar pattern at convenience store chains 7-Eleven and Circle K.

items.title: Stellantis stock rises 13% as automaker's turnaround plan, cost cuts gain traction
items.summary: European car giant Stellantis said Wednesday that it recorded a 4 billion euro ($4.5 billion) cash shortfall in the third quarter.
items.body: Shares of Stellantis were up Wednesday as the European car giant's third-quarter results showed it was making progress with its 60 billion euro turnaround plan. Third-quarter revenues rose 1% to 37.6 billion euros from a year ago, the Chrysler and Jeep owner said on Wednesday, while adjusted operating income rose 184% to 256 million euros from 90 million euros a year earlier. The automaker's industrial free cash flow improved to negative 4 billion euros, up from negative 4.3 billion the year prior. Stellantis on Wednesday also reconfirmed its 2026 guidance and target to achieve positive free cash flow next year, which is a main focus for investors. "Q3 was soft, but consensus expectations were far lower.

items.title: 'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones
items.summary: As drone deliveries become more commonplace, their makers are looking for ways to make them quieter.
items.body: Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland. She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads. It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders. "They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant. "You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says. Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.

items.title: Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world
items.summary: The chancellor is right to focus on pure affordability, but £100 handouts and delayed decisions won’t shield consumers from the next wave of price hikes Amid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher…
items.body: A mid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher energy prices that have resulted from the Iran war have pushed up inflation, are eating into households’ incomes, are a drag on businesses – and are the main reason why the forecast for GDP growth next year was cut from 1.6% to just 1%. And energy was the focus of Healey’s sole surprise in his consumer-facing policies – the £100 payment to 20m households in A-D council tax bands to help with fuel bills this winter. It will be funded, in effect, by tapping the banks for a few quid for 15 months via the bank surcharge. But the chancellor will know that £100 won’t look generous when the bills land.

items.title: Looking for yield? This could be one of the best times in recent market history to buy corporate bonds
items.summary: This could be one of the best times to buy corporate bonds in recent history, investing experts say, with treasuries yielding 5% boosting fixed income market.
items.body: Looking for yield? Investing experts say now may be one of the best moments in recent market history to buy corporate bonds. With the 10-year Treasury yield still flirting around 5% and the Federal Reserve holding rates steady at its FOMC meeting on Wednesday, fixed income experts say the environment for highly rated investment-grade corporates is attractive — some have called it a "generational opportunity." Leading the market are hyperscalers including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, companies that have been aggressively issuing debt for artificial intelligence projects, including buying chips and building data centers and power plants to run them.

items.title: Restaurants sceptical over 'garlic and gherkins' plan
items.summary: Import tariffs on more than 100 items - including garlic, gherkins and plant-based milk - are being removed.
items.body: Garlic, gherkins and plant-based milk are among more than 100 products which should become cheaper due to measures announced in the Budget. The Treasury said the removal of import tariffs on dozens of items would save the typical household about £21 a year on their food bill. But some businesses have questioned how much difference it will make to them, suggesting that VAT cuts or moves to make it cheaper for them to employ staff would have been better. Morgan Austin, from burger chain Burgerism, which has six main locations and first opened in Salford in 2018, said the removal of tariffs on gherkins was good news. "Really appreciate the gherkins - that is fantastic for us," said the 26-year-old operations manager. But she said she would have liked to see more significant support for hospitality businesses, including a VAT reduction.

items.title: Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget | Aditya Chakrabortty
items.summary: The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment Was this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of…
items.body: W as this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of neoliberalism”? Fat chance. Was it John Healey’s budget – the repair job of a cautious chancellor fretting about record-high taxes, £3tn of public debt and an economy stuck in first gear? Little sign of that. This budget was cast in the image of a man who isn’t in Burnham’s government or even a Labour politician – but who appears almost every day on TV, on podcasts and is probably better known than 649 of the MPs at Westminster. Today’s budget was the Martin Lewis budget. Lewis is the MoneySavingExpert , whose weekly Money Tips email advises 10 million British subscribers on cheap mortgages, Black Friday deals and how to score two pizzas for £10. Tips and tricks to stave off rising prices and make the most of the money you have.

items.title: Trump is using tariffs as a 'tool for grift,' Raskin says in demand for donor records
items.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin wrote to President Trump in the final days of a midterm election cycle where government corruption has emerged as a top issue for voters.
items.body: A top House Democrat on Wednesday accused President Donald Trump of using tariffs as a "tool for grift and self-enrichment," pointing to what he says are suspicious import-tax exemptions for industries whose leaders have curried Trump's favor with gifts and donations . "You took care to cut lots of sweetheart deals with corporations and industries that won carve-outs from your tariffs when you saw you could get something good in return," Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told Trump in a fiery letter obtained first by CNBC. Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the former top Democrat on the House oversight committee, highlighted three such tariff carve-outs — for Brazilian meat , diamonds and smartphones — that he says "make little to no sense" under the criteria set by the Trump administration.

items.title: The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps | Editorial
items.summary: Banks, landlords and gambling firms will pay more as the chancellor begins building a fairer economy and a more active state in a cost of living crisis John Healey’s first budget was a Rorschach test. Supporters saw dozens of measures offering “ breathing space” to a public worn…
items.body: J ohn Healey’s first budget was a Rorschach test. Supporters saw dozens of measures offering “ breathing space” to a public worn down by rising prices. Critics admitted to a slew of announcements but countered that each was modest in value . Underlying both views is that the budget was more ambitious on how a state can do more to protect the public than on how much it spends. The chancellor has taken a small step in the right direction – a tricky feat in a turbulent world. But an economy marked by entrenched inequality and more than a decade of stagnation will need a bigger stride. The Office for Budget Responsibility’s “ pretty grim picture ” of living standards exposes the budget’s central weakness: its relief is temporary, while the squeeze on households persists.

items.title: Options traders break down a massive Alphabet trade into earnings
items.summary: The market's mini rally faces a key test after the bell when tech giants Alphabet and Microsoft report.
items.body: Options traders took contrasting views on Alphabet as the hyperscaler gets set to report earnings after the close. Current options prices are implying a nearly 6% move, well about its eight quarter median move of 2.6%. Traders were decidedly bullish heading into the first. Just before noon, a trader bought 2271 contracts of the 350/365 call spread for about $4.4. The trade target a move higher to $365, a 13% jump from its current price. The trade is a bet the in the near term, the worst is behind Alphabet, which has seen its shares fall nearly 20% from its all time highs reached back in May. This is a trade that looks to take advantage of high near-term volatility in Alphabet's shorter dated puts. The goal is for those short-dated puts to expire worthless, with the trader then long the 300-strike puts, looking for a 9% move lower through mid January.

items.title: Japan's Nidec misses deadline to obtain unqualified audit opinion
items.body: TOKYO/KYOTO -- Japanese motor maker Nidec announced on Wednesday that the company has not yet obtained an unqualified audit opinion on its annual securities report. Its auditor PwC Japan has informed the company that it will not be able to complete its audit in time.

items.title: He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harm | John Crace
items.summary: Armed with 98 measures, a rictus grin and a decidedly comedy-free speech, the chancellor at least offered us – and Labour – some breathing space It was as if John Healey was taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can…
items.body: I t was as if John Healey was taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can all think of plenty of chancellors who have done untold damage. Take a bow George Osborne. It might just have been better if the doctor that Healey had chosen to impersonate was not Dr Death. John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed. Not everyone can have a naturally sunny disposition. His face seems to be carved out of despair. But it would be a big help if, when called upon to make his most important speech of the year, he didn’t reinforce the impression when he opened his mouth. A one-way journey to the slough of despond. “I’m very sorry to let you know, Mr Crace,” he would say with Voldemort delight. “But your cancer is now terminal.

items.title: Anthropic IPO filing warns some risks may be uninsurable. AI coverage will be issue for every company
items.summary: Anthropic warned the market there may not be enough insurance in the world to covers its AI risks. To less extreme degrees, it's an issue all companies face.
items.body: Anthropic's IPO filing includes many words covering many risks , from IP theft to security incidents, data loss, climate change, rogue agents and all the way to an existential crisis for humanity. Embedded in all of the risk language are basic questions about insurance: What's going to be covered? Is it even possible to provide a policy for all of the ways that AI could go wrong? Anthropic, even with more cash than almost any company in America, couldn't answer that question with confidence. "Because our models may behave in ways that no user or developer intended, claims arising from such actions could result in substantial liability. Our insurance policies also may not provide sufficient coverage to adequately mitigate the potential liabilities we face, especially where any one incident, or a group of incidents, causes disproportionate harm," the company's S-1 filing states .

items.title: Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel responds | Panel
items.summary: Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough? Continue reading...
items.body: Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough? First, he did no harm. Then he scattered sprinkles of feel-goods. He told the truth about the state we’re in, deep in an extra £14bn of expensive debt , and, though he put it politely, at the mercy of the monster in the White House’s whims on Iran and tariffs. The losers were popular targets: the banks and gambling companies. But plainly bank threats to decamp partly paid off. Their shares leapt up on the news that their surcharge would rise to only 6%, not its original 8% before Tory reductions. They expected to pay more, and indeed they should.

items.title: Oil prices rise as U.S. reportedly tells Gulf countries to prepare for Iran strikes after midterm elections
items.summary: Oil prices climbed Wednesday as investors weighed the prospect of a prolonged conflict in the Middle East.
items.body: Crude oil prices climbed Wednesday, as the U.S. is reportedly preparing to renew strikes against Iran after the midterm elections. International benchmark Brent crude futures rose 1.3% to close at $115.32 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 2.9% to settle at $102.78 per barrel. The U.S. has told several Gulf Arab countries to be ready for a short but intense military campaign after the midterms, people briefed on the conversations told The Wall Street Journal . President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said that the war with Iran would end on his terms , while insisting that Tehran must be prevented from acquiring nuclear weapons. Speaking at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday, Trump said the conflict could be brought to a swift conclusion but stressed that any agreement must ensure Iran would never possess a nuclear weapon.
